summary:
Manitoba stands under the framework of Canada. Federal protections for gender identity and gender expression apply in Manitoba as they do across the country, and the province's own Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public and private accommodations.

As of March 2025 the Manitoba NDP government had a bill before the Legislative Assembly to extend the Human Rights Code to cover gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe stated the change would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing; the bill was scheduled for debate later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba's executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it. Until the amendment is passed, gender expression is not a named prohibited ground in Manitoba's provincial code, though federal protections and Charter interpretation still apply.

Manitoba has enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level. In May 2024 the legislature passed a bill recognizing March 31 as the Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a transgender backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park. The province has raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, most recently in November 2023, an observance first marked eight years earlier; that year's flag was raised by Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara issued a statement that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans.

Manitoba recorded the joint-lowest provincial police-reported hate-crime rate in Canada for 2024, at 5.3 per 100,000, alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, against a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba was among the eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining, recording no increase in 2024 while the national total rose 1% to 4,882 incidents. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and Statistics Canada's release breaks out motivations by category rather than establishing trans-specific hate-crime volume.

Legal gender recognition in Manitoba follows the provincial rules that apply across Canada, with vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson, speaking at the 2023 Remembrance observance, said the day memorializes people murdered as a result of transphobia and that this violence shows no sign of slowing.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-provincial policy turbulence elsewhere in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport and primarily affects minors and residents rather than visitors. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or their gender identity, prompting human rights calls for repeal and litigation. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, the Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from court challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause. Manitoba has not enacted comparable school or sport restrictions.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, with explicit inclusion as a prohibited ground completed as of 2017. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. The concepts of sex under section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement, with courts required to interpret human rights statutes consistently with the Charter.

National context relevant to a visitor's expectations: Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults in 2022 and made it a crime under the Criminal Code; same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since July 2005; and the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologised in December 2020 for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, creating an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify and mitigate implicit bias in policing practices. A poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020 found 87.6% would be comfortable having a transgender neighbour, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour. Canada ranked first in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023 and first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024.

Whether gender expression is a named provincial ground therefore depends on the bill's passage, which is not established in the sources.

Residents can access the Manitoba human rights complaint route for discrimination on gender identity, and Charter section 15 protections binding all laws and government institutions, including law enforcement, apply to provincial authorities. Vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates are under provincial jurisdiction, and legal gender change is available under Manitoba's provincial rules.

Provincial government observances include the legislatively enacted Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility on March 31, passed in May 2024 on a bill from Logan Oxenham, and the annual transgender flag raising in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, most recently in November 2023. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara have publicly stated government support for the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans.
outOfScopeNotes:
The passage of Manitoba's gender-expression amendment to the Human Rights Code is unresolved in the sources: the bill was before the legislature as of March 2025 with debate scheduled for later that year, and no source confirms enactment.

Statistics Canada's 2024 hate-crime release reports Manitoba's rate of 5.3 per 100,000 as the joint-lowest provincial figure, but the release does not break out gender-identity motivation, so trans-specific hate-crime volume in Manitoba is not established. Police-reported data capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of national police data including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations, is referenced as the underlying document for the national statistics; its Manitoba-specific findings are not detailed in the inventory.

No Manitoba-specific incident of violence against a trans person, no Manitoba correctional-placement case, and no Manitoba-specific legal gender recognition refusal or approval is documented in the sources.
